lessons.title: Printing in Java
objectives: distinguish between System.out.print and System.out.println behavior
interpret escape sequences in printed text
predict the result of string concatenation mixed with numeric addition

steps.code: System.out.println("Hello, world!");

points.text: The command that prints. Spelled exactly like this — capital S, lowercase println.
points.label: System.out.println

points.text: Whatever sits inside the double quotes is what appears. Java does not read it, it just prints it.
points.label: the quotes

points.text: Ends the instruction. Every line like this needs one.
points.label: the semicolon

points.text: The ln on the end means "then go to a new line".
points.label: ln

steps.instruction: This is how you put something on the screen.

steps.code: System.out.println("Hello, world!");
steps.after: You just ran your first program. The computer did exactly what the line said.
steps.instruction: This is a Java program. Run it.

steps.code: System.out.println("Hello, world!");
steps.hint: Change only the words between the quotes.
steps.after: Your words, on the screen. That's programming.
steps.instruction: Change the message to anything you want. Run it.

points.text: Prints and STAYS on the line. The next print carries on right after it.
points.label: print

points.text: Prints and ENDS the line. Anything after it starts fresh below.
points.label: println

points.text: Three separate commands, one line of output — because the first two were print.
points.label: HiBye!

steps.instruction: print and println differ by one thing: the new line.

steps.why: println = print line: it ends the line after printing. Two printlns → two lines.
steps.code:
System.out.println("Hi");
System.out.println("Bye");
steps.instruction: What comes out?

steps.why: print doesn't end the line — the next print continues right where it left off.
steps.code:
System.out.print("Hi");
System.out.print("Bye");
steps.instruction: Same code — but print, no ln. Now what?

steps.code:
System.out.print("Java");
System.out.print("rocks");
steps.hint: Which one ends the line — print or println?
steps.after: println ends the line; print doesn't. That's the whole difference.
steps.instruction: Make it match the target.

steps.output:
one
two
name	score
She said "hi"
back \ slash

points.text: A new line, right where you put it — even in the middle of one message.
points.label: \n

points.text: A tab. Useful for lining columns up.
points.label: \t

points.text: A real quote mark. Without the backslash it would end your text early and break.
A single backslash. You need two because one backslash always means "something special follows".

steps.instruction: A backslash gives you characters you cannot just type.

steps.code: System.out.println("one\ntwo\nthree");
steps.after: \n means new line — even in the middle of one message.
steps.instruction: One line of code. Run it and watch the \n.

steps.why: \t prints a tab — a wide gap. Great for lining things up.
steps.code: System.out.println("name\tscore");
steps.instruction: What does \t do?

steps.code: System.out.println("She said "hi" to me");
steps.hint: Quotes inside quotes confuse Java. \" means: print a real quote mark.
steps.after: \" prints a quote without ending the text. Errors point at the problem — reading them is a skill.
steps.instruction: It's broken. Run it, read the error, fix it.

points.text: Between pieces of text, + joins them. It adds no space — you add your own.
points.label: gluing

points.text: Left to right. "1"+2 is already text, so 3 gets glued on: 123.
Left to right again. 1+2 is real maths first (3), THEN the text joins: 33.
Once text is involved, + stops adding and starts gluing.
points.label: the rule

steps.instruction: The + sign glues text together.

steps.why: Left to right: "1"+2 makes the TEXT "12", then "12"+3 makes "123". Once text joins in, + glues.
steps.code: System.out.println("1" + 2 + 3);
steps.instruction: The classic. What prints?

steps.why: Still left to right: 1+2=3 (real math — no text yet), then 3+"3" glues into "33".
steps.code: System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3");
steps.instruction: Flip it. Now what prints?

steps.hint: print keeps going on the same line. println ends it.
steps.after: print + println together control exactly how output flows.
steps.instruction: Tap the lines in order to match the target.

steps.code: // your code here
steps.hint: One println per line, and \t for the gap.
steps.after: You wrote a real program from scratch. Everything on this receipt, you now control.
steps.instruction: Your turn. Print this receipt — match it exactly.

lessons.title: Variables and Types
objectives: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name
use = to put a value in, and change it later
choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: We're building a player card.

points.label: the card
points.text: Five facts about one player: their name, their level, their health, their rank, and whether they are online.

points.label: the problem
points.text: Each fact is a different KIND of thing. A name is text. A level is a whole number. Health can be half a heart.

points.label: a variable
points.text: A labelled box that holds one fact. You put a value in once, then use the label wherever you need it.

points.label: how we go
points.text: One box at a time. The card grows on screen, and by the end you have built the whole thing.

steps.instruction: First fact: the name. Text goes in a String.

points.label: String name
points.text: The type goes in FRONT of the name you choose. That is what creates the box.

points.label: = "Ada"
points.text: The = does not mean "equals". It means "put this in". The text goes into the box.

points.label: String
points.text: Capital S. Holds text of any length, in double quotes.

points.label: + name
points.text: No quotes around name, so Java uses what is INSIDE the box, not the word name.

steps.instruction: Run it. That is the first line of the card.
steps.after: One box made, one line printed.

steps.instruction: Make the player Grace instead.
steps.hint: Only the text inside the quotes changes.
steps.after: One edit changed the card. The label stayed the same.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Next fact: the level. Whole numbers go in an int.

points.label: int level
points.text: Same shape as before: type, name, =, value.

points.label: int
points.text: Whole numbers only. 7, 0, -3. No decimal point.

points.label: no quotes
points.text: 7 is a number, so it needs no quotes. "7" with quotes would be text.

points.label: the card grows
points.text: Two boxes now, two lines of card.

steps.instruction: The player levels up. Changing a box is not the same as making one.

points.label: int level = 7;
points.text: Type in FRONT, so this MAKES the box. This is called declaring, and you do it once.

points.label: level = 8;
points.text: No type. The box already exists, so this only puts a new value in.

points.label: the 7 is gone
points.text: A box holds one value. Putting 8 in throws the 7 away — it does not add up.

points.label: int level = 8;
points.text: Writing that second line WITH the type would be an error: you cannot make the same box twice.

steps.instruction: What does this print?
steps.why: The second line replaces what is in the box. It does not add — 7 and 8 never meet.
skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Next fact: health. Half a heart will not fit in an int.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5

points.label: the problem
points.text: Health is 2.5 hearts. An int has nowhere to keep the .5, so it cannot hold it.

points.label: double
points.text: Works exactly like int, but it keeps the decimal part.

points.label: which to pick
points.text: int for what you COUNT: levels, lives, coins. double for what you MEASURE: health, height, money.

points.label: still fine
points.text: A double can hold a whole number too. It just shows it as 3.0 instead of 3.

steps.instruction: This one refuses to run. Fix the type.
steps.code:
int health = 2.5;
System.out.println("Health: " + health);
steps.solution:
double health = 2.5;
System.out.println("Health: " + health);
steps.hint: 2.5 has a decimal point. Which type keeps that?
steps.after: Java refused rather than quietly losing your .5. That refusal is it protecting you.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Next fact: the rank, a single letter.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Rank:   A

points.label: char
points.text: Exactly ONE character. A letter, a digit, a symbol — one.

points.label: 'A'
points.text: SINGLE quotes. 'A' is a char. "A" with double quotes would be a String.

points.label: why bother
points.text: A rank is always one letter, so char says so exactly. A name could be any length, so it stays a String.

steps.instruction: Last fact: are they online? That is a yes or a no.
steps.output:
=== PLAYER CARD ===
Name:   Ada
Level:  7
Health: 2.5
Rank:   A
Online: true

points.label: boolean
points.text: Holds only true or false. Nothing else is allowed in the box.

points.label: lowercase, no quotes
points.text: true, not True, and not "true" — quotes would make it text.

points.label: card complete
points.text: Five facts, five types. Every one chosen because of what it had to hold.

steps.instruction: Run the finished card.
steps.after: You built that from one line. Five boxes, five kinds of value.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Now the exact rules, so they hold up in a test.

points.label: four parts
points.text: Every declaration is: TYPE, NAME, =, VALUE. In that order, ending in a semicolon.

points.label: declare once
points.text: The type appears only the first time. After that, just name = value.

points.label: capitals matter
points.text: level and Level are two different boxes. Java will not guess what you meant.

points.label: quotes decide the type
points.text: "A" is a String. 'A' is a char. A is a variable name. Same letter, three meanings.

steps.instruction: Which type holds each value?
steps.why: Whole number → int. Decimal → double. One character in single quotes → char. Text in double quotes → String. true/false → boolean.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Two the test always asks.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a type Java has?
questions.why: int, double, char and boolean are all built into Java. apple is just a word — Java has never heard of it.

questions.prompt: Which line both MAKES a box and puts a value in?
questions.why: It has all four parts: type, name, =, value. The second only changes an existing box; the third has no name; the fourth is just text.

skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: Put the right type in front of each name.
steps.hint: Text in double quotes, then a whole number.
steps.after: Type in front, every time.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: This will not run. Look carefully at the capitals.
steps.code:
int Level = 7;
System.out.println("Level:  " + level);
steps.solution:
int level = 7;
System.out.println("Level:  " + level);
steps.hint: Level and level are two different names as far as Java is concerned.
steps.after: One capital letter is enough to break it. Java never guesses.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

steps.instruction: a = b copies the value. Follow it.

questions.why: a = b copies what is currently in b, which is 2.
Still 2. Copying took the value, not the box — changing b later does nothing to a.

skills: use = to put a value in, and change it later

steps.instruction: Fill in the two missing values so it prints the card below.
steps.hint: Text needs double quotes. A whole number needs none.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.2.5, Answering Questions.
skills: choose between int, double, char, boolean and String for a given value

steps.instruction: Last one: store the year in an int, then print the sentence.
steps.code: // declare an int called year, then print it
steps.solution:
int year = 2026;
System.out.println("The current year is " + year);
steps.hint: Type, name, =, value. Then join text and the box with a +.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.2.4, Our First Integer. Lesson done.
skills: declare a variable by putting its type in front of its name

lessons.title: User Input
objectives: read user input using the Scanner class
choose the right Scanner method for each input type
prompt the user before reading input

steps.code:
String favColor = readLine("Hello, what is your favorite color? ");
System.out.println(favColor);
steps.output:
Hello, what is your favorite color? blue
blue

points.text: Asks your question and hands back whatever the user typed, as text.
points.label: readLine

points.text: The question goes INSIDE the brackets. You don't print it separately.
points.label: the prompt

points.text: A box to keep the answer in, so you can use it later.
points.label: String favColor

points.text: The first line is the question with your answer typed after it. The second is what println printed.
points.label: two lines

steps.instruction: Programs can ask the person using them a question.

steps.code:
String favColor = readLine("Hello, what is your favorite color? ");
System.out.println(favColor);
steps.after: The program waited, took the answer, and used it.
skills: read text from the user with readLine
steps.instruction: Run it. We'll type "blue" for you.

steps.code:
String favColor = readLine("Hello, what is your favorite color? ");
System.out.println(favColor);
steps.hint: Change the words inside the quotes.
steps.after: You decide exactly what it asks.
skills: read text from the user with readLine
steps.target:
Hello, what is your favorite color? blue
blue
steps.instruction: Change the question it asks. Run it.

points.text: Text — a name, a colour, a sentence. Gives back a String.
points.label: readLine

points.text: A whole number, like an age. Gives back an int, so you can do maths with it.
points.label: readInt

points.text: A decimal number, like a price or a distance. Gives back a double.
points.label: readDouble

points.text: true or false. Gives back a boolean.
points.label: readBoolean

points.text: All of them take the question as the thing in brackets.
points.label: all four

steps.instruction: There are four ways to read input, one per kind of answer.

steps.why: The name tells you what kind of answer it expects, and what type of box you need to store it in.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
steps.instruction: Match each one to what it reads.

steps.code:
int age = readInt("Hello, how old are you? ");
System.out.println(age + 1);

points.text: Gives back a real number, so age + 1 does maths and prints 17.
points.label: readInt

points.text: The box has to match what you asked for: a whole number goes in an int.
points.label: int age

points.text: You'd get the text "16", and age + 1 would glue instead of add.
points.label: if you used readLine

steps.instruction: Reading a number so you can calculate with it.

steps.why: What you type appears right after the question, on the same line. And because readInt gives a number, age + 1 is maths (17), not gluing (161).
steps.code:
int age = readInt("How old are you? ");
System.out.println("Next year: " + (age + 1));
opts:
How old are you? 16
Next year: 17

How old are you?
16
Next year: 17

How old are you? 16
Next year: 161
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
steps.instruction: The user typed 16. What appears?

steps.code:
String name = readInt("What is your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.hint: A name is text, not a number. Which of the four reads text?
steps.after: The method has to match the kind of answer — and the box has to match the method.
skills: choose between readLine, readInt, readDouble and readBoolean
steps.target:
What is your name? Ada
Hi, Ada!
steps.solution:
String name = readLine("What is your name? ");
System.out.println("Hi, " + name + "!");
steps.instruction: This asks for a name but reads it the wrong way. Fix it.

steps.code: // ask with readDouble, then print
steps.hint: Miles can have a decimal, so use readDouble and store it in a double.
steps.after: Ask, store, use. That's every input program you'll write.
skills: use a value the user typed in your program
steps.target:
How many miles have you traveled? 2.5
5.0
steps.solution:
double miles = readDouble("How many miles have you traveled? ");
System.out.println(miles * 2);
steps.instruction: Ask how many miles they travelled, then print it doubled.

lessons.title: Arithmetic Expressions
objectives: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
predict the result of integer division
use the modulo operator to find remainders

points.text: Add, subtract, multiply. * is a star, not an ×.
Divide. It behaves differently for whole numbers than you expect — that's coming up.
Remainder. 7 % 2 is 1, because 2 goes into 7 three times with 1 left over.
Brackets, to force what happens first.

steps.instruction: Java does maths with these six symbols.

steps.after: Exactly like a calculator. The interesting part is next.
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
steps.instruction: Run it. Nothing surprising yet.

steps.code: System.out.println(2 + 3 * 4);

points.text: * and / and % happen BEFORE + and -. Same rule you already use in maths class.
points.label: first

points.text: 2 + 3 * 4 is 2 + 12, which is 14. It is NOT 5 * 4.
points.label: so

points.text: Put brackets around what you want to happen first.
points.label: override

steps.instruction: When there's more than one operator, order matters.

steps.why: Brackets go first, so it's 5 * 4 = 20. Without them it would have been 14.
steps.code: System.out.println((2 + 3) * 4);
skills: evaluate arithmetic expressions using order of operations
steps.instruction: Brackets added. Now what?

steps.code: System.out.println(7 / 2);

points.text: When BOTH numbers are whole numbers, Java throws away the fraction. It does not round.
points.label: 3, not 3.5

points.text: A whole number divided by a whole number has to stay a whole number. 3.5 can't fit, so the .5 is dropped.
points.label: why

points.text: Gives 4, not 4.5 and not 5. Always chops downward.
Make one of them a decimal: 7.0 / 2 gives 3.5.
points.label: want 3.5?

steps.instruction: Now the one that catches everybody.

steps.why: Both are whole numbers, so the .5 is thrown away and you get 4.
steps.code: System.out.println(9 / 2);
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: So what does this print?

steps.why: The division happens FIRST, as whole numbers, giving 4. Only then is 4 stored in a double. Storing it in a double afterwards can't bring the .5 back — it prints 4.0.
steps.code:
double avg = 9 / 2;
System.out.println(avg);
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.instruction: This one looks safe but isn't. Tap the line that goes wrong.

steps.code:
double avg = 9 / 2;
System.out.println(avg);
steps.hint: One of the two numbers has to be a decimal BEFORE the division happens.
steps.after: Making one side a decimal changes the whole sum to decimal maths.
skills: predict the result of integer division
steps.solution:
double avg = 9.0 / 2;
System.out.println(avg);
steps.instruction: Make it print the real average, 4.5.

points.text: 2 fits into 7 three times (6), and 1 is left over. So 1.
5 fits exactly, nothing left over. So 0.
A remainder of 0 means it divides evenly — that's how you test if a number is even, or a multiple of anything.
points.label: 0 means

steps.instruction: % gives you what's left over.

steps.code:
System.out.println(20 % 6);
System.out.println(20 % 4);
skills: use the modulo operator to find remainders

questions.why: 4 fits exactly 5 times, nothing left over.

steps.instruction: Work these out.

points.text: Short for score = score + 1. Adds one.
points.label: score++

points.text: Short for score = score - 1. Takes one away.
points.label: score--

points.text: Short for score = score + 5. There is -= and *= and /= too.
points.label: score += 5

points.text: Same meaning, less typing. You will see these constantly once loops start.
points.label: why bother

steps.instruction: Shortcuts for changing a number you already have.

steps.hint: One of them counts how many fit. The other is what refuses to fit.
steps.after: / tells you how many fit. % tells you what is left. Together they split any number.
skills: predict the result of integer division
use the modulo operator to find remainders
steps.instruction: Fill it in so it splits 17 into boxes of 5.

steps.code:
int totalSeconds = 200;
// print: 3 min 20 sec
steps.hint: / 60 gives the whole minutes. % 60 gives the seconds left over.
steps.after: Whole part with /, leftover with %. Same trick for time, money, anything.
skills: predict the result of integer division
use the modulo operator to find remainders
steps.solution:
int totalSeconds = 200;
System.out.println(totalSeconds / 60 + " min " + totalSeconds % 60 + " sec");
steps.instruction: Your turn: turn 200 seconds into minutes and seconds.

lessons.title: Casting
objectives: turn a double into an int with (int)
use (double) to stop whole-number division
round a number to the nearest whole number using casting

points.text: The type you want, in brackets, in front of the value.
points.label: (int)

points.text: 9.9 becomes 9. It does NOT round — everything after the point is thrown away.
points.label: chops

points.text: Still 9. Even 9.999999 is 9. Casting never rounds up.
points.label: 9.99 too

points.text: The result is a whole number, so it goes in an int.
points.label: the box

steps.instruction: (int) turns a decimal into a whole number by chopping.

steps.after: The .9 is gone, not rounded.
steps.instruction: Run it.

steps.why: Casting chops. 3.99 loses everything after the point and becomes 3, even though it is nearly 4.
steps.code: System.out.println((int) 3.99);
skills: turn a double into an int with (int)
steps.instruction: What prints?

points.text: Two ints, so Java does whole-number division. 3 / 4 is 0 with 3 left over — you get 0.
points.label: a / b

points.text: Turns 3 into 3.0 BEFORE the divide, so it becomes decimal division.
points.label: (double) a

points.text: The answer you actually wanted.
Only one side has to be a double. The other is converted automatically.
points.label: one is enough

steps.instruction: (double) rescues you from whole-number division.

steps.after: The types decided the answer, not the numbers.
skills: use (double) to stop whole-number division
steps.instruction: Run it. Same two numbers, two different answers.

steps.code:
System.out.println((double) (3 / 4));
System.out.println((double) 3 / 4);

points.text: Brackets first. 3 / 4 already happened as ints and gave 0. Casting 0 gives 0.0 — too late.
points.label: (double) (3 / 4)

points.text: The cast lands on the 3 first, so the division is decimal from the start. 0.75.
points.label: (double) 3 / 4

points.text: Cast BEFORE the division, not after. Rescuing a lost answer is impossible.
points.label: the rule

steps.instruction: Where you put the cast changes everything.

steps.why: 7 / 2 is done first as ints and gives 3. Casting that gives 3.0 — the .5 was already thrown away.
steps.code: System.out.println((double) (7 / 2));
skills: use (double) to stop whole-number division
steps.instruction: Which one gives 0.0?

points.text: 3.7 + 0.5 is 4.2. Chopping 4.2 gives 4. Rounded up, using only chopping.
points.label: the trick

points.text: 3.4 + 0.5 is 3.9. Chopping gives 3. Rounded down, correctly.
points.label: rounding down

points.text: 3.5 + 0.5 is 4.0, which chops to 4 — .5 rounds up, the way you were taught.
points.label: exactly .5

points.text: The + 0.5 must happen first, so it needs its own brackets inside the cast.
points.label: the brackets

steps.instruction: Add 0.5, then chop — that is how you round.

steps.hint: Nudge it up by half, then let the chop decide.
steps.after: 3.4 + 0.5 is 3.9, which chops to 3. The nudge is not big enough to reach 4.
skills: round a number to the nearest whole number using casting
steps.instruction: Fill it in so 3.4 rounds to 3 and 3.7 would round to 4.

steps.code: // read a double, round it with casting, print "Rating rounded: N"
steps.hint: Prompt is "Please enter a movie rating: ". Then add 0.5 and cast to int.
steps.after: That is CodeHS exercise 3.5.8, Movie Ratings.
skills: round a number to the nearest whole number using casting
steps.target:
Please enter a movie rating: 3.5
Rating rounded: 4
steps.instruction: Your turn: read a movie rating and round it to the nearest whole star.

lessons.title: Booleans
objectives: create boolean variables that hold true or false
tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number
read a true/false answer from the user

points.text: The type. A box that can only ever hold true or false.
points.label: boolean

points.text: The only two values there are. All lowercase, and never in quotes.
points.label: true / false

points.text: There is no third option. That is the whole point of a boolean.
points.label: no maybe

points.text: Naming it like a yes/no question makes the code read like English later.
points.label: isRaining

steps.instruction: A boolean holds one of exactly two things.

steps.after: Two boxes, two answers.
steps.instruction: Run it.

steps.hint: Change the value, not the type.
steps.after: You set them. Later the program will work them out for itself.
skills: create boolean variables that hold true or false
steps.instruction: Make it print false twice.

points.text: Both print true. Quotes never appear in the output, so you cannot tell them apart by looking.
points.label: identical output

points.text: A boolean. Java understands it as a yes.
points.label: true

points.text: A String. Four letters of text that happen to spell true. Java cannot reason with it.
points.label: "true"

points.text: 'T' is a char and 10.1 is a double. Only bare true and false are booleans.
points.label: watch out

steps.instruction: true and "true" look the same on screen. They are not the same.

steps.why: Bare true/false → boolean. Double quotes → String. Single quotes around one character → char. A decimal number → double.
skills: tell a boolean apart from text, a character and a number
steps.instruction: Which type is each one?

steps.code:
boolean isStudent = readBoolean("Are you a student? ");
System.out.println(isStudent);
steps.output:
Are you a student? true
true

points.text: Asks your question and hands back true or false.
points.label: readBoolean

points.text: The user has to type the word true or the word false.
points.label: they type

points.text: It gives back a boolean, so it has to go in a boolean.
points.label: the box

steps.instruction: You can ask the user a yes/no question.

steps.code:
